chapters.title: The Gathering
paragraphs: APOLLODORUS: Yes, friend, and the reason people say I'm crazy and out of my mind is precisely because I hold these views about you and me. No other evidence is needed.
COMPANION: Enough of that, Apollodorus. Just tell me about the conversation, as I asked.
APOLLODORUS: Well, the story about love went like this — but perhaps I should start from the beginning and try to give you the exact words of Aristodemus.
He said he ran into Socrates, freshly bathed and wearing sandals — which was unusual — so he asked where he was going, all dressed up like that.

'To a dinner party at Agathon's,' he replied. 'I turned down his invitation yesterday — I was afraid of the crowd — but I promised to come today instead. So I've put on my best clothes, since he's such a fine man. What do you say — want to come along, uninvited?'
'Whatever you say,' I replied.
'Follow me, then,' he said, 'and let's turn the old proverb on its head:'
'To the feasts of lesser men, the good come uninvited.'
Instead, our version will be:
'To the feasts of the good, the good come uninvited.'

And we can back this up with Homer himself, who not only overturns the proverb but outright mocks it. After portraying Agamemnon as the bravest of men, he has Menelaus — a far less impressive warrior — show up uninvited to Agamemnon's feast. So the lesser man comes to the greater man's table, not the other way around.
'I'm a bit worried, Socrates,' said Aristodemus, 'that I'll be more like Menelaus — the lesser man who shows up uninvited to a wise man's dinner.'
'To the feasts of the wise, the inferior goes uninvited.'
But I'll say you invited me, and then you'll have to make an excuse for me.
'Two heads are better than one,'
he replied, quoting Homer. 'Between us, we'll come up with something on the way.'

That was the style of their conversation as they walked. Then Socrates fell into one of his fits of abstraction, and told Aristodemus, who was waiting for him, to go on ahead. When Aristodemus arrived at Agathon's house, he found the doors wide open. A servant came out, met him, and led him straight to the banquet hall where the guests were already reclining, the meal about to begin. 'Welcome, Aristodemus!' said Agathon as soon as he appeared. 'You're just in time for dinner. If you've come for any other reason, put it off and join us — I was looking for you yesterday and meant to invite you if I could find you. But where's Socrates?'
I turned around, but Socrates was nowhere to be seen. I had to explain that he'd been with me just a moment ago, and that I'd come at his invitation.
'Good of you to come,' said Agathon, 'but where is he?'
'He was right behind me as I came in,' Aristodemus said. 'I can't imagine what's happened to him.'
'Go look for him, boy,' said Agathon to a servant, 'and bring him in. Aristodemus, take the place next to Eryximachus.'

The servant helped him wash and get settled. Soon another servant came in and reported that Socrates had wandered into the neighbor's porch. 'He's standing there,' the servant said, 'and when I called him, he wouldn't move.'
'How odd,' said Agathon. 'Call him again — keep calling.'
'Leave him alone,' said Aristodemus. 'He does this — he stops somewhere and loses himself in thought for no apparent reason. I'm sure he'll come in soon. Don't disturb him.'

'Well, if you think so, I'll leave him,' said Agathon. Then, turning to the servants: 'Let's eat without waiting for him. Serve whatever you like — no one's giving orders tonight. Pretend that you're our hosts and we're your guests. Take good care of us, and we'll praise you for it.' Dinner was served, but still no Socrates. Agathon kept wanting to send for him, but Aristodemus objected. Finally, when the meal was about half over — Socrates' trances were never very long — he came in. Agathon, who was reclining alone at the end of the table, invited him to sit beside him. 'Come lie next to me,' he said, 'so I can touch you and absorb the wise thought that came to you in that porch. I'm sure you wouldn't have stopped until you found what you were looking for.'

'If only wisdom could flow by touch,' said Socrates, taking his place, 'from the full person to the empty one, the way water flows through wool from a full cup to an empty one! If that were so, I'd be thrilled to lie next to you — your wisdom would fill me with its brilliance and beauty, while mine is dim and doubtful, no better than a dream. Yours shone with the splendor of youth the day before yesterday, in front of more than thirty thousand Greeks.'
'You're making fun of me, Socrates,' said Agathon. 'We'll settle who's really wiser soon enough — let Dionysus be the judge. But for now, eat your dinner.'

Socrates took his place and ate with the others. After the meal, they poured libations, sang a hymn to the god, and performed the usual ceremonies. They were about to start drinking when Pausanias spoke up: 'Friends, how can we drink without doing ourselves damage? I can tell you that I'm still feeling yesterday's party, and I need time to recover. I suspect most of you are in the same state — you were all there too. So how can we make tonight's drinking easier?'
'I completely agree,' said Aristophanes. 'We should definitely avoid heavy drinking. I was absolutely drowning in wine yesterday.'
'You're right,' said Eryximachus, the physician and son of Acumenus. 'But let me hear from one more person — Agathon, can you handle serious drinking?'
'Absolutely not,' said Agathon.

'Then it seems,' said Eryximachus, 'that we light drinkers — myself, Aristodemus, Phaedrus, and others who can never hold their liquor — are in luck, since even the strong drinkers aren't in the mood tonight. I won't include Socrates, who can drink or abstain equally well and won't mind either way. Since none of us seems inclined to drink heavily, let me say as a doctor that deep drinking is harmful. I never do it if I can help it, and I certainly don't recommend it to anyone, especially someone still recovering from last night.'
'I always follow your advice,' said Phaedrus, 'especially your medical advice — and the rest of the company will too, if they're wise.'
Everyone agreed: tonight would not be about heavy drinking. They would each drink only as much as they pleased.

'Excellent,' said Eryximachus. 'Since we've agreed that drinking will be voluntary, with no pressure, let me propose that we dismiss the flute-girl — she can go play for herself or for the women in the other rooms. Tonight, let's have conversation instead. And if you'll permit me, I'll suggest a topic.' Everyone accepted this proposal, so Eryximachus continued:
'I'll begin,' he said, 'by quoting Euripides:',
'The words I speak are not my own —'

they come from Phaedrus. He often says to me, quite indignantly: 'Isn't it strange, Eryximachus, that while other gods have poems and hymns composed in their honor, the great god Love has never received a single proper tribute from all our many poets? And think of the sophists — Prodicus, for instance, has written eloquent prose about Heracles and other heroes. Someone even wrote an inspired essay on the usefulness of salt! All sorts of trivial subjects have been celebrated in elaborate speeches, yet no one has ever dared to properly praise Love. Such a mighty god, so completely neglected!' Phaedrus is absolutely right, and so I want to make a contribution to Love's honor — and I think this is the perfect occasion. I propose that each of us, going from left to right, make a speech praising Love — the best speech he can manage. Phaedrus should go first, since he's sitting on the far left and since the whole idea is his.

'No one will vote against you, Eryximachus,' said Socrates. 'How could I object, when I claim to understand nothing but love? Agathon and Pausanias won't disagree either, and certainly not Aristophanes, whose whole life revolves around Dionysus and Aphrodite. The proposal might seem harder for those of us who speak last, but we'll be happy as long as the first speakers do a good job. Let Phaedrus begin his praise of Love — and good luck to him!' Everyone agreed and urged him to start.
Aristodemus didn't remember everything that was said, and I don't remember everything he told me. But I'll tell you what I found most worth remembering — what the main speakers said.

chapters.title: Phaedrus's Speech
paragraphs: Phaedrus began by declaring that Love is a great and wondrous god, marvelous among both gods and mortals — especially remarkable for how he came into being. He is the oldest of the gods, which is a mark of honor. The proof? No poet or writer has ever named his parents. As Hesiod says:
'First came Chaos, and then broad-bosomed Earth, the eternal foundation of all things, and Love.'
In other words, after Chaos came Earth and Love — these two, the first beings. Parmenides sings of it too:
'Love was the first god created.'

Acusilaus agrees with Hesiod. So many authorities confirm that Love is the eldest of the gods. And being the eldest, he is the source of our greatest blessings. I can think of no greater advantage for a young person starting out in life than a worthy lover, nor for a lover than a beloved worth loving. The principle that should guide anyone who wants to live nobly — this principle cannot be instilled by family ties, honors, wealth, or anything else as well as it can by love. What principle? The sense of honor and shame, without which neither cities nor individuals accomplish anything great. A lover caught acting shamefully will feel more pain at being seen by his beloved than by his father, friends, or anyone else. The same goes for the beloved. If there were some way to create an army entirely of lovers and their beloveds, they would be the best possible rulers of their city, shunning all dishonor and competing with each other in virtue. Fighting side by side, even a small force of lovers could conquer the world.

What lover would not rather be seen by the whole world than by his beloved, either abandoning his post or throwing down his weapons? He would choose to die a thousand deaths. Who would desert his beloved or fail him in the hour of danger? The worst coward would become as brave as the bravest hero, inspired by Love. The courage that Homer says the gods breathe into certain warriors — Love breathes naturally into every lover.

Love alone makes people willing to die for others — and this applies to women as well as men. Alcestis, daughter of Pelias, proved it to all of Greece. She was willing to die for her husband when no one else would — not even his own father and mother. Her love so surpassed theirs that they seemed like strangers rather than parents. The gods were so moved that they granted her something almost unheard of: the right to return from the dead. Even the gods honor the devotion that love inspires. But Orpheus the musician was sent away empty-handed — they showed him only a phantom of his dead wife, not the real woman. They punished his cowardice. Unlike Alcestis, he didn't dare to die for love; instead, he tried to sneak into the underworld alive. Later, they had him torn apart by women as punishment.

Very different was the reward for Achilles' true love of his friend Patroclus. Achilles was the lover, not the beloved — the idea that Patroclus was the beloved is a foolish mistake by Aeschylus, since Achilles was clearly the more beautiful, more beautiful than all the heroes, and as Homer tells us, still beardless and much younger. While the gods greatly honor the virtue of love, they admire even more the devotion of the beloved who loves the lover in return — because the lover, being inspired by a god, is more divine. Achilles knew perfectly well — his mother had told him — that he could avoid death and live to old age if he didn't kill Hector. But he gave his life to avenge his friend, daring to die not just in Patroclus's defense but even after Patroclus was already dead. For this, the gods honored him even above Alcestis and sent him to the Islands of the Blessed. This is why I say that Love is the oldest, noblest, and most powerful of the gods — and the greatest source of virtue in life and happiness after death.

chapters.title: Pausanias's Speech
paragraphs: This, or something close to it, was Phaedrus's speech. Several other speeches followed that Aristodemus couldn't remember, but the next one he recounted was Pausanias's. Pausanias began: Phaedrus, I don't think the question has been framed correctly. We shouldn't be asked to praise Love in such an undiscriminating way. If there were only one Love, what you said would be fine — but since there are more Loves than one, we should have started by deciding which of them we are praising. Let me fix this oversight. First I'll tell you which Love deserves our praise, and then I'll try to hymn that praiseworthy one in a manner worthy of him. For we all know that Love is inseparable from Aphrodite, and if there were only one Aphrodite there would be only one Love — but since there are two goddesses, there must be two Loves. And am I not right that there are two goddesses? The elder, who has no mother, is called the heavenly Aphrodite — she is the daughter of Uranus. The younger, the daughter of Zeus and Dione, we call Common; and the Love who works alongside her is rightly named Common, just as the other Love is called Heavenly. All the gods deserve praise, but not without distinguishing their natures — so I must try to distinguish the characters of the two Loves. Now, actions vary in value according to how they are performed.

Take, for example, what we are doing right now — drinking, singing, and talking. These actions are not in themselves either good or evil; they turn out one way or the other depending on how they are done. Done well, they are good; done badly, they are evil. In the same way, not every love is noble and worthy of praise — only the love that has a noble purpose. The Love who is the offspring of the Common Aphrodite is essentially common and makes no distinctions. It is the love the meaner sort of men feel, directed equally at women and at youths, and it is of the body rather than the soul. The most foolish beings are the objects of this love, which cares only about getting what it wants and never about achieving its end nobly, and so it does good and evil quite indiscriminately. The goddess who is his mother is far younger than the other, and she was born of the union of male and female, partaking of both. But the offspring of the Heavenly Aphrodite comes from a mother in whose birth the female had no part — she is from the male only. This is the love that is directed toward youths, and because the goddess is older, there is nothing of wantonness in her. Those inspired by this love turn to the male, delighting in whoever has the more valiant and intelligent nature; and anyone can recognize the pure enthusiasts by the very character of their attachments.

For they love not boys, but intelligent beings whose reason is beginning to develop — around the age when their beards begin to grow. And in choosing young men as their companions, they mean to be faithful to them, to spend their whole lives with them — not to catch them in their inexperience, deceive them, play the fool with them, or run from one to another. The love of young boys, however, ought to be forbidden by law, because their future is uncertain: they may turn out good or bad, in body or soul, and much noble enthusiasm may be wasted on them. In this matter the good are a law to themselves, but the coarser sort of lovers ought to be restrained by force — just as we try to restrain them from fixing their affections on freeborn women. These are the people who bring reproach upon love; and some have been led to deny the lawfulness of such attachments altogether because they see the impropriety and evil in them. But surely nothing done decorously and lawfully can justly be censured.

Now here in Athens, and in Lacedaemon, the rules about love are perplexing, but in most cities they are simple and easy to grasp. In Elis and Boeotia, and in countries that have no gift for eloquence, the rules are very straightforward — the law is simply in favor of these connections, and no one, young or old, says a word against them. The reason, I suppose, is that the men there are not eloquent, so lovers prefer not to take the trouble of pleading their case. In Ionia, on the other hand, and in other places generally subject to the barbarians, the custom is held to be dishonorable. There, love between males shares the evil reputation attached to philosophy and gymnastics, because all three are hostile to tyranny. Rulers' interests require that their subjects be poor in spirit and that no strong bond of friendship or fellowship form among them — and love, more than any other motive, is likely to inspire such bonds, as our own Athenian tyrants learned by experience. For the love between Aristogeiton and the steadfast devotion of Harmodius proved strong enough to bring down their power.

And so the ill repute into which these attachments have fallen in some places must be attributed to the bad character of those who condemn them — that is, to the self-seeking of the rulers and the cowardice of the ruled. On the other hand, the indiscriminate honor given to them in other countries is owing to the mental laziness of those who hold that opinion. In our own country a far better principle prevails, though, as I said, it's a rather perplexing one. Consider: open loves are held to be more honorable than secret ones, and the love of the noblest and highest is especially honorable, even when the beloved is less beautiful than others. Consider too the enormous encouragement the whole world gives the lover: he is not thought to be doing anything dishonorable — if he succeeds he is praised, and if he fails he is blamed. And in pursuing his love, custom allows him to do many strange things that philosophy would bitterly condemn if they were done from any motive of profit, or desire for office, or power.

He may pray, beg, supplicate, swear oaths, sleep on a mat at the door, and endure a servitude worse than any slave's. In any other situation his friends and enemies alike would step in to stop him; but here no friend will be ashamed of him or admonish him, and no enemy will accuse him of meanness or flattery. The actions of a lover have a grace that ennobles them, and custom has decided they are highly commendable and bring no loss of character. And strangest of all, he alone may swear and forswear himself — so people say — and the gods will forgive his transgression, for there is no such thing as a lover's oath. Such is the complete liberty that gods and men have allowed the lover, according to the custom that prevails in our part of the world. From this point of view a man could fairly argue that in Athens to love and to be loved is considered a most honorable thing. But then again — when fathers forbid their sons to speak with their lovers and place them under a tutor whose job is to prevent any such thing, and when their companions and peers taunt them for anything of the sort they observe, and their elders refuse to silence these reproaches or rebuke them — anyone reflecting on all this would, on the contrary, conclude that we hold these practices to be utterly disgraceful.

But as I was saying at the start, the truth, I think, is this: whether such practices are honorable or dishonorable is not a simple question. They are honorable to whoever pursues them honorably, and dishonorable to whoever pursues them dishonorably. There is dishonor in yielding to the bad, or yielding in a bad way; but there is honor in yielding to the good, or yielding in an honorable way. Evil is the vulgar lover, who loves the body rather than the soul — he isn't even stable, because he loves something that is itself unstable, so when the bloom of youth he desired is gone, he takes wing and flies away, breaking all his words and promises. But the love of a noble disposition lasts a lifetime, for it becomes one with what is everlasting. The custom of our country would have both lover and beloved thoroughly tested — have us yield to the one sort of lover and avoid the other, and therefore it encourages some to pursue and others to flee, testing both the lover and the beloved in contests and trials until it becomes clear which class each of them belongs to.

This is why, in the first place, a hasty attachment is considered dishonorable: time is the true test, here as in most other things. And secondly, there is dishonor in being overcome by the love of money, wealth, or political power — whether a man is frightened into surrender by the fear of losing them, or, having tasted the benefits of money and political corruption, cannot rise above their seductions. For none of these things is permanent or lasting, and besides, no generous friendship ever sprang from them. There remains, then, only one honorable way for the beloved to yield — the way of virtue. For just as we granted that any service the lover renders to his beloved is not to be counted as flattery or as a dishonor to himself, so the beloved has one, and only one, form of voluntary service that is not dishonorable: namely, virtuous service.

For we have a custom according to which, if someone serves another in the belief that he will be improved by him — whether in wisdom or in some other particular of virtue — such voluntary service is not to be considered a dishonor, and it is not open to the charge of flattery. These two customs — the love of youth, and the practice of philosophy and virtue generally — ought to meet in one; and when they do, the beloved may honorably yield to the lover. For when lover and beloved come together, each following his own law: the lover thinking he is right to do any service he can for his gracious loved one, and the beloved thinking he is right to show any kindness he can to the one who is making him wise and good — the first capable of communicating wisdom and virtue, the second seeking to acquire them for the sake of his education and wisdom — then, when the two laws of love are fulfilled and meet in one, and only then, may the beloved yield honorably to the lover. And when love is of this disinterested sort, there is no disgrace in being deceived; but in every other case there is equal disgrace in being deceived or not. For if someone yields to a lover under the impression that he is rich, and is then disappointed of his gains because the lover turns out to be poor, he is disgraced just the same — because he has shown that for money's sake he would give himself up to anyone, for any base use; and that is not honorable.

By the same principle, a man who gives himself to a lover because he believes him to be a good man, hoping to be improved by his company, shows himself to be virtuous even if the object of his affection turns out to be a scoundrel with no virtue at all. If he is deceived, his error is a noble one. For he has proved that on his side he will do anything for anyone with a view to virtue and self-improvement — and nothing can be nobler than that. Noble, then, in every case, is the acceptance of another for the sake of virtue. This is the love of the Heavenly Goddess — heavenly love, of great worth to individuals and to cities, making lover and beloved alike earnest in the work of their own improvement. All other loves are the offspring of the other goddess, the Common one. To you, Phaedrus, I offer this contribution of mine in praise of Love, the best I could make on short notice.

Pausanias came to a pause — this is the balanced way of speaking I've been taught by the wise. Aristodemus said that Aristophanes was supposed to speak next, but either from eating too much or for some other reason he had the hiccups and had to switch turns with Eryximachus the physician, who was reclining on the couch just below him. Eryximachus, he said, you ought either to cure my hiccups or speak in my turn until they stop.

I'll do both, said Eryximachus. I'll speak in your place, and you can speak in mine; and while I'm speaking, let me recommend you hold your breath. If after a while the hiccups haven't gotten better, then gargle a little water; and if they still persist, tickle your nose with something and sneeze — once or twice should do it, and even the most violent hiccups are sure to stop. I'll do as you prescribe, said Aristophanes. Now get on with it.

chapters.title: Eryximachus's Speech
paragraphs: Eryximachus began: 'Since Pausanias started well but ended rather weakly, I'll try to pick up where he left off. He was right to distinguish two kinds of Love. But my medical training tells me that this double Love extends far beyond the human soul's attraction to beauty — it's present in the bodies of all living things, in the products of the earth, in practically everything that exists. Medicine has taught me how vast and universal Love's domain truly is, extending over all things both divine and human. Let me begin with medicine, to honor my profession. The human body contains both kinds of love — they're clearly different and unlike each other, with different desires. The desire of the healthy body is one thing; the desire of the sick body is another. As Pausanias said that it's honorable to gratify good people and dishonorable to gratify bad ones — so too in the body, the healthy elements should be gratified and encouraged, while the diseased elements should not.'

That, in essence, is what medicine is: the knowledge of what the body loves and desires, and how to satisfy those desires or not. The best doctor can distinguish healthy desire from unhealthy desire, and knows how to convert one into the other — how to create desire where it's needed and remove it where it's harmful, reconciling the body's most hostile elements and making them work in harmony. The most opposed elements are things like hot and cold, bitter and sweet, wet and dry. My ancestor Asclepius founded our art by learning how to create friendship and harmony among these opposites. The poets confirm this, and I believe them. Not just medicine, but athletics and farming operate on the same principles. And anyone who pays attention will see that music works the same way — it's all about reconciling opposites. That's probably what Heraclitus meant when he said 'The One is united through its own opposition, like the harmony of bow and lyre' — though his wording was a bit confused. It's absurd to say that harmony is discord or is made of things that are still in conflict.

What he probably meant was that harmony arises from notes that were once different — higher and lower pitches that once clashed — but have been brought into agreement by the art of music. If the higher and lower notes still disagreed, there could be no harmony. Harmony is agreement, and agreement between things that disagree is impossible as long as they still disagree. Rhythm works the same way — it's composed of short and long elements, once different, now in accord. In all these cases, just as medicine reconciles the body's opposites, music creates love and unity among sounds. Music, too, is concerned with the principles of love applied to harmony and rhythm. In the abstract nature of harmony and rhythm, recognizing love is straightforward. But when you try to use these principles in actual life — composing songs or performing existing pieces correctly — that's where it gets difficult, and where a skilled artist is needed.

The old lesson must be repeated: Heavenly Love — the love of the Heavenly Muse Urania — is beautiful and must be cultivated with care. Its purpose is to make the undisciplined disciplined and to preserve those who already are. But Common Love — that of Polyhymnia — must be handled cautiously. Pleasure should be enjoyed without becoming license, just as a good doctor regulates an epicure's appetite so he can enjoy food without getting sick. In music, medicine, and everything else both human and divine, both loves must be carefully observed, for both are present.

Even the seasons reflect these two principles. When the elements of hot and cold, wet and dry achieve harmonious love and blend in proper proportion, they bring health and plenty to humans, animals, and plants. But when the unruly Love takes control of the seasons, it causes enormous destruction — plagues, blights, frost, and hail all spring from the excess and disorder of these elemental loves. The study of these forces in relation to the movements of the stars and the seasons is what we call astronomy. Furthermore, all religious sacrifice and divination — the art of communication between gods and humans — is concerned with preserving good love and curing bad love. Every kind of impiety follows when people honor the wrong Love instead of the right one, whether in their feelings toward gods, parents, the living, or the dead. Divination's job is to identify and heal these loves. Divination is the peacemaker between gods and humans.

The love that is directed toward what is good, and perfected alongside temperance and justice — whether among gods or humans — has the greatest power. It's the source of all our happiness and harmony, and it makes us friends with both the gods above and with each other. I've probably left out things that could be said in praise of Love, but not on purpose. Aristophanes, you can fill in whatever I've missed, or take a completely different approach — I notice your hiccups seem to be gone.

'Yes,' said Aristophanes, 'they're gone — but only after I used the sneezing trick. It makes me wonder whether the body's sense of harmony has a fondness for such ridiculous noises and tickling. The sneezing cured me instantly.'

'Be careful, Aristophanes,' said Eryximachus. 'You're making jokes before you've even started your speech. Now I'll have to keep watch to see if I can laugh at you — when you could have spoken in peace.'

'You're right,' laughed Aristophanes. 'Let me take back what I said. But please don't watch me too closely. My worry isn't that my speech will be funny — that's my muse's natural style, and the funnier the better. My worry is that people will laugh at me rather than with me.'
'You think you can take a shot and then escape, Aristophanes? Well, be very careful and remember that you'll be held accountable — though maybe, if you behave, I'll let you off.'

chapters.title: Aristophanes's Speech
paragraphs: Aristophanes announced that he would take a completely different approach. 'Humanity,' he said, 'has never truly understood the power of Love — judging by how little attention we pay him. If we understood Love, we would surely have built him magnificent temples and altars and made grand sacrifices. But none of this has been done, though it certainly should be, because Love is the best friend humanity has — our helper and healer, the one who cures the very ills that stand between us and happiness. Let me describe his power, and you can teach the rest of the world. First, you need to understand what human nature was like originally, because it was very different from now. To begin with, there were three sexes, not two: man, woman, and a third combining both — the androgynous, which once really existed but is now just a word of ridicule. Second, the original humans were round — their backs and sides forming a circle. They had four hands, four feet, one head with two faces looking in opposite directions on a round neck, four ears, two sets of private parts, and everything else to match.'

They could walk upright in either direction, forwards or backwards. And when they wanted to move fast, they'd cartwheel — spinning on all eight limbs like acrobats tumbling with their legs in the air. There were three sexes because each was the offspring of a different celestial body: men came from the sun, women from the earth, and the androgynous from the moon, which partakes of both sun and earth. Like their parents, the originals were round and moved in circles. They were tremendously strong, and their ambitions were enormous — they even attacked the gods. The story of Otus and Ephialtes, who tried to scale heaven and assault the gods, is told about them. The gods held an anxious council. Should they destroy the humans with thunderbolts, as they'd done with the giants? But then they'd lose all the worship and sacrifices. They couldn't let the insolence continue either. Finally Zeus had an idea: 'I think I have a plan that will humble their arrogance while letting them survive. I'll cut each one in two — they'll be weaker but more numerous, and more profitable to us.'

'They'll walk upright on two legs. And if they keep misbehaving, I'll split them again, and they'll have to hop around on one leg.' He then cut them in two, the way you'd slice an apple for preserving, or split an egg with a hair. After each cut, he told Apollo to turn the face and half the neck around so people could see their own cut side — that would teach them humility. Apollo healed their wounds and shaped their new forms. He pulled the skin together over what we call the belly, like a drawstring purse, and fastened it at the center — we call it the navel. He smoothed out most of the wrinkles, like a cobbler smoothing leather, though he left a few around the belly as a reminder. After the splitting, each half desperately sought its other half. When they found each other, they threw their arms around one another and clung together, longing to merge back into one. They started dying of hunger and neglect, because they refused to do anything apart. When one half died, the survivor searched for another mate — whether the half of an original man or woman — and clung to that.

The race was in danger of dying out when Zeus, taking pity, devised another solution: he moved their reproductive parts to the front. Previously, humans had reproduced by sowing seed in the ground, like grasshoppers. After the rearrangement, reproduction happened through the union of male and female. If a man found a woman, they could produce children and continue the race. If a man found a man, they would at least find satisfaction and relief, and then get on with the business of living. So ancient is the desire we feel for one another — it goes all the way back to our original nature. Love is the name for the desire and pursuit of wholeness. Each of us, when separated, is like a flat fish — just one half of a person, always looking for the other half. Men who are halves of the original androgynous being are attracted to women; women who are halves of the original woman are attracted to other women; and men who are halves of the original man are attracted to other men.

Some people call these last ones shameless, but that's wrong. They act not from shamelessness but from boldness and courage — they're drawn to what resembles them. The proof: when they grow up, these are the only ones who enter politics. When someone — of any type — meets their actual other half, the effect is overwhelming. The pair are struck with an astonishing sense of love, friendship, and closeness, and they refuse to be separated for even a moment. These are the people who spend their whole lives together — yet they can't explain what they really want from each other. It's clearly not just physical intimacy; the soul wants something it can sense but can't articulate.

Imagine Hephaestus, the smith god, standing over them with his tools as they lie together, and asking: 'What is it you two really want from each other?' If they couldn't answer, he might say: 'Is it this — to be so completely united that you're never apart, day or night? If so, I can melt you together into a single being. While alive, you'd share one life. After death, in the underworld, you'd still be one soul instead of two. Is that what you want?' Not a single person would say no. Everyone would recognize that this — merging into one, becoming whole again — is the deepest, oldest human longing. The desire and pursuit of this wholeness is what we call Love. Once we were whole; now, because of our wrongdoing, the gods have scattered us — the way the Spartans broke up Arcadia into separate villages.

And if we continue to defy the gods, we risk being split again — left to go around like figures in a bas-relief, with only half a nose. So let us urge everyone to respect the gods, so that we may avoid further punishment and find what Love promises: our true other half. This is rare in the present world, but Love is our guide and commander. No one should oppose Love — to do so is to oppose the gods. If we are at peace with Love, we will find our true companions, which almost never happens now. I'm being serious, so please, Eryximachus, don't make fun of what I've said or look for veiled references to Pausanias and Agathon. My point is universal — it applies to all men and women everywhere. If our loves were perfectly fulfilled, and each of us found our original other half, the human race would be happy. And if perfection is impossible, then the next best thing is finding someone truly compatible.

Therefore, if we want to praise the one who gives us this blessing, we must praise Love — our greatest benefactor, who leads us back toward our own nature in this life and gives us hope for the next. Love promises that if we honor the gods, he will restore us to our original wholeness and heal us and make us happy. This, Eryximachus, is my discourse on Love. It's different from yours, but I beg you not to ridicule it, so that everyone can have their turn. Or rather, so that Agathon and Socrates can have theirs — since they're the only ones left.

'I won't attack you,' said Eryximachus. 'I thought your speech was charming. And if I didn't know that Agathon and Socrates are masters of love, I'd worry they'd have nothing left to say. But I'm not worried.'
Socrates said: 'You performed well, Eryximachus. But if you were in my position — or rather, the position I'll be in after Agathon speaks — you'd be terrified.'
'You're trying to jinx me, Socrates,' said Agathon, 'so I'll be rattled by the audience's expectations.'

'I'd have to be very forgetful, Agathon,' replied Socrates, 'of the courage you showed when your plays were about to be performed — stepping onto the stage with the actors, facing a vast theater without the slightest fear — if I thought a small group of friends could make you nervous.'
'Do you think, Socrates,' said Agathon, 'that I'm so stage-struck I don't know that a few wise judges are far more intimidating than a crowd of fools?'

'I wouldn't dream of accusing you of such a lack of refinement, Agathon. I know perfectly well that if you happened to meet someone you considered truly wise, you'd care more about his opinion than about the crowd's. But we — we were part of that foolish crowd in the theater, so we don't count as wise. Still, I know that if you found yourself in the presence of a genuinely wise person, you'd be embarrassed to disgrace yourself — wouldn't you?'
'Yes,' said Agathon.
'But you wouldn't be embarrassed doing something disgraceful in front of a crowd?'

Here Phaedrus interrupted: 'Don't answer him, dear Agathon! If he gets a partner to argue with — especially a good-looking one — he'll forget about everything else. I love listening to Socrates argue, but right now we need him and everyone else to pay their tribute to Love. Once you've both given your speeches, then you can argue.'

'You're absolutely right, Phaedrus,' said Agathon. 'There's no reason I can't give my speech — I'll have plenty of other chances to talk with Socrates. Let me explain my approach first, and then speak.'

chapters.title: Agathon's Speech
paragraphs: The previous speakers, instead of actually praising Love or revealing his nature, seem to have congratulated humanity on the benefits Love provides. But I'd rather first praise the god himself, then describe his gifts — that's the proper way to praise anything. I say — without disrespect — that of all the blessed gods, Love is the most blessed because he is the fairest and the best. And he is the fairest because, first of all, he is the youngest. Love himself is proof of this: he flees from old age — which moves faster than most of us would like — and Love wants nothing to do with it. Youth and love live together, like to like, as the saying goes. I agree with much of what Phaedrus said, but not that Love is older than Kronos and Iapetus. No — I say he is the youngest of the gods, forever youthful. The ancient conflicts among the gods that Hesiod and Parmenides describe — if those stories are true — were caused by Necessity, not Love. If Love had existed then, there would have been no chains, no mutilations, no violence among the gods — only peace and gentleness, as there has been in heaven ever since Love began his reign. Love is young, and also tender. He deserves a poet like Homer to celebrate his tenderness, as Homer wrote of the goddess Ate:
'Her feet are tender, for she steps not on the ground but on the heads of men.'

A fine proof of her tenderness — she walks not on hard surfaces but on soft ones. We can make a similar argument for Love: he doesn't walk on the earth, or even on human skulls (which aren't particularly soft), but in the hearts and souls of gods and mortals — the softest things of all. In them he walks, makes his home, and dwells. Not in every soul — wherever he finds hardness, he departs; wherever he finds softness, he stays. Nestling always in the softest of soft places, he must be the softest of beings. He is not only the youngest and most tender, but also the most flexible — otherwise he couldn't wrap himself around everything or slip in and out of every soul unnoticed. His grace proves his flexibility, for grace is universally recognized as Love's special quality; gracelessness and love are eternal enemies. The beauty of his complexion is revealed by where he lives — among flowers and fragrances, never amid fading beauty of body or soul. Where there are flowers and scents, there Love sits and stays. About the beauty of the god, I've said enough — though much more could be said.

Now I must speak of Love's virtue. His greatest glory is that he neither commits nor suffers any wrong — neither from any god nor any mortal. He doesn't suffer by force, because force cannot touch him. He doesn't act by force either, because everyone serves Love willingly. And where there is voluntary agreement, there is justice — as the city's laws declare. Love is not only just but supremely temperate: Temperance rules over pleasures and desires, and no pleasure masters Love — he masters them all. If he conquers every pleasure, he must be temperate indeed. As for courage, even the God of War is no match — Love is Ares' master, not his servant, because love conquered even the bravest god. If Love conquers the bravest of all, he must be the bravest himself. I've spoken of his courage, justice, and temperance. Now I must address his wisdom, as best I can. First, he is a poet — and here, like Eryximachus, I praise my own art — and the source of poetry in others. He must be a poet himself, since no one can give what they don't have or teach what they don't know.

Everyone Love touches becomes a poet, even if they had no music in them before. This proves that Love is a master of all the fine arts — you can't give what you don't possess. Who will deny that Love created all living things? Aren't all creatures born and begotten through Love's wisdom? And among artists, we know that only those whom Love inspires achieve lasting fame — those untouched by Love walk in darkness. The arts of medicine, archery, and prophecy were all discovered by Apollo under Love's guidance. The music of the Muses, Hephaestus's metalwork, Athena's weaving, Zeus's rule over gods and mortals — all came from Love, the inventor of these arts. Love brought order to the realm of the gods through the love of beauty, since Love has nothing to do with ugliness. In the old days, as I said, terrible things happened among the gods because they were ruled by Necessity. But since Love was born — born of the love of beauty — every good thing in heaven and earth has followed. Therefore, Phaedrus, I declare that Love is the fairest and best in himself, and the cause of all that is fairest and best in everything else. A line of poetry comes to mind — Love is the god who
'Gives peace on earth and calms the stormy deep, who stills the winds and lets the troubled sleep.'

He empties people of hostility and fills them with affection. He brings us together at gatherings like this — at festivals, feasts, and dances. He is our lord. He gives us courtesy and takes away discourtesy. He gives kindness and never unkindness. Friend of the good, wonder of the wise, marvel of the gods. Desired by those who don't have him, cherished by those who do. Parent of grace, desire, tenderness, and softness. He regards the good and disregards the bad. In every word, every deed, every wish, every fear — he is our savior, guide, companion, and helper. The glory of gods and mortals, the best and brightest leader. Let every person follow in his footsteps, singing sweetly in his honor, joining in the song with which Love charms the souls of all who hear. That is my speech, Phaedrus — partly playful, partly serious — dedicated to the god, as best as I'm able.

When Agathon finished, Aristodemus said the whole company cheered. The young man was thought to have spoken in a way worthy of both himself and the god. Socrates looked at Eryximachus and said: 'Well, son of Acumenus — wasn't I right to be worried? Wasn't I prophetic when I said Agathon would give a magnificent speech and leave me in trouble?'
'You were right about Agathon being magnificent,' replied Eryximachus. 'But not about you being in trouble.'

'My dear friend,' said Socrates, 'how can anyone not be in trouble when they have to speak after hearing such a rich and dazzling speech? I was especially stunned by the beauty of the closing words — who could hear them without amazement? When I considered how immeasurably inferior my own abilities are, I was ready to run away in shame, if there had been any escape. The speech reminded me of Gorgias, and at the end I felt as though Agathon were pointing Gorgias's head at me — turning me to stone and striking me dumb, just like Medusa in Homer. Then I realized how foolish I'd been to agree to take a turn praising Love, boasting that I was a master of the subject. I'd naively assumed that a proper speech of praise should be truthful — that you start with what's true and select the best truths to present in the best way. I felt quite confident, thinking I knew how to praise properly. But now I see the real plan was to heap every possible form of greatness and glory upon Love, whether truthfully or not — truth didn't matter. The original proposal wasn't that we should actually praise Love, but that we should appear to praise him.

So you attributed to Love every conceivable form of praise you could find anywhere, declaring 'he is all this' and 'causes all that,' making him appear the fairest and best to people who don't know him — though you can't fool those who do. A noble and solemn hymn of praise! But since I misunderstood the rules when I agreed to participate, my promise was — as Euripides might say — a promise of the lips, not the mind. Forget that kind of praise; I won't do it. But if you'd like to hear the truth about Love, spoken in my own way, with whatever words come to me — I'm ready. Phaedrus, would that be acceptable to you?

Aristodemus said that Phaedrus and the company told Socrates to speak however he thought best. 'Then,' Socrates added, 'let me first ask Agathon a few questions, so I can build my speech on his answers.'
'Ask away,' said Phaedrus. 'I give you permission.' And so Socrates began.

chapters.title: Socrates & Diotima
paragraphs: In the magnificent speech you just gave, dear Agathon, I think you were right to begin by describing Love's nature before discussing his works — that's an approach I really approve of. Since you've spoken so eloquently about his nature, may I ask you one more thing: Is love the love of something, or of nothing? I don't mean is it the love of a father or mother — that would be silly. I mean: just as we'd say a father is a father of something — of a son or daughter — is Love the love of something?
'Of course,' said Agathon.
'And you'd say the same of a mother?'
He agreed.
'Let me ask one more question to make my meaning clear: Isn't a brother essentially a brother of something?'
'Certainly,' he replied.
'Of a brother or sister?'
'Yes,' he said.
'Now,' said Socrates, 'I'll ask about Love: Is Love the love of something, or of nothing?'
'Of something, certainly,' he replied.
'Keep that in mind, and tell me this: Does Love desire the thing it loves?'
'Yes, surely.'
'And does Love possess what it loves and desires, or not?'
'Probably not, I'd say.'

'Think carefully,' replied Socrates. 'Isn't "necessarily" more accurate than "probably"? The principle that whoever desires something must lack that thing — that whoever desires nothing lacks nothing — is absolutely and necessarily true, Agathon. Don't you agree?'
'I agree,' said Agathon.
'Good. Would a tall person desire to be tall, or a strong person desire to be strong?'
'That would contradict what we just agreed.'
'Exactly. Someone who already is something can't desire to become it.'
'Very true.'

'And yet,' added Socrates, 'if a strong person said they desired to be strong, or a healthy person said they desired to be healthy, you might think they desired something they already had. I bring this up to avoid confusion. These people, Agathon, necessarily have these qualities right now, whether they want them or not. So who would desire what they already have? When someone says "I'm healthy and I want to be healthy" or "I'm rich and I want to be rich," we should tell them: "You already have health, wealth, and strength. What you really desire is to keep having them in the future." In other words, you desire something you don't yet have — namely, the continuation of what you have now. He'd have to agree, wouldn't he?'
'He would,' replied Agathon.
'Then,' said Socrates, 'this person desires to preserve for the future something not yet available to them — something they don't yet have.'
'Very true,' he said.

'So everyone who desires, desires what they don't already have — what is future, not present, what they lack, what they are not, what they are without. These are the sorts of things that love and desire seek, aren't they?'
'Very true,' he said.
'Now,' said Socrates, 'let's review the argument. First: isn't love always the love of something? And second: isn't it the love of something that a person lacks?'
'Yes,' he replied.

'Now recall what you said in your speech — or if you've forgotten, I'll remind you: you said that the love of beauty brought order to the realm of the gods, because no one loves what is ugly. Didn't you say something like that?'
'Yes,' said Agathon.
'And rightly so, my friend. If that's true, then Love must be the love of beauty, not of ugliness?'
He agreed.
'And we've established that Love desires what it lacks, what it doesn't have?'
'True,' he said.
'Then Love lacks beauty and does not possess it?'
'Necessarily,' he replied.
'And would you call something beautiful that lacks beauty and doesn't possess it?'
'Certainly not.'
'Then can you still say that Love is beautiful?'
'I'm afraid I didn't know what I was saying,' Agathon replied.
'It was a very fine speech, Agathon,' replied Socrates. 'But let me ask one more small question: Isn't the good also beautiful?'
'Yes.'
'Then if Love lacks beauty, and if the good is beautiful, Love must also lack the good?'
'I can't argue with you, Socrates. Let's say you're right.'
'Say rather, dear Agathon, that you can't argue with the truth. Arguing with Socrates is easy enough.'

Now, leaving you behind, let me tell you a story about love that I once heard from Diotima of Mantineia — a woman wise in this and many other things. Years ago, when the Athenians made sacrifices before the plague struck, she managed to delay the disease by ten years. She was my teacher in the art of love, and I'll repeat what she told me, starting from the same conclusions I just reached with Agathon — which are nearly identical to the ones I reached with her. I'll play both parts myself. As you suggested, Agathon, I should speak first about Love's nature and being, then about his works. I told her, in much the same words you used, that Love was a great god, and also beautiful. She proved to me — just as I proved to you — that Love is neither beautiful nor good. 'What do you mean, Diotima?' I said. 'Is Love ugly and evil?' 'Hush!' she cried. 'Must everything that isn't beautiful be ugly? And must everything that isn't wise be ignorant? Don't you see there's a middle ground between wisdom and ignorance?' 'What would that be?' I asked.

'True belief,' she replied. 'True belief, as you know, can't give reasons for itself — so it isn't knowledge (how could knowledge lack reasons?). But it isn't ignorance either, because it grasps the truth. It's something between ignorance and wisdom.' 'That's right,' I said. 'Then don't insist,' she said, 'that whatever isn't beautiful must be ugly, or that whatever isn't good must be evil. Don't assume that because Love isn't beautiful or good, he must therefore be ugly and evil. He's in between.' 'But,' I said, 'everyone agrees that Love is a great god.' 'Everyone who knows, or everyone who doesn't?' 'Everyone!' 'And how,' she said with a smile, 'can Love be acknowledged as a great god by those who say he isn't a god at all?' 'Who says that?' I asked. 'You and I, for two,' she replied. 'How so?' 'Easy. You'd agree that all gods are happy and beautiful — wouldn't you? You wouldn't dare say any god was not?' 'Of course not,' I said. 'And by happy, you mean those who possess good and beautiful things?' 'Yes.' 'But you've admitted that Love, because he lacks these things, desires the good and beautiful things he doesn't have.' 'I did.' 'Then how can he be a god if he has no share in what is good or beautiful?' 'He can't, apparently.' 'So you see — you too deny Love's divinity.'

'Then what is Love?' I asked. 'Is he mortal?' 'No.' 'What then?' 'As before — he's neither mortal nor immortal, but something in between.' 'What is he, Diotima?' 'A great spirit — a daimon. Like all spirits, he stands between the divine and the mortal.' 'And what is his power?' I asked. 'He interprets between gods and humans,' she replied, 'carrying prayers and sacrifices from us up to the gods, and commands and rewards from the gods down to us. He bridges the gap that separates divine from mortal, and through him all communication between gods and humans takes place — whether we're awake or asleep. Through Love flow prophecy, priestly arts, sacrifice, mystery, incantation, and every form of divination and sorcery. God does not mix directly with humanity; all interaction between the divine and the human passes through Love. The wisdom that grasps this is spiritual wisdom; all other wisdom — the technical skills of crafts and trades — is ordinary and vulgar. These spirits are many and diverse, and Love is one of them.' 'Who were his parents?' I asked. 'The story takes some telling,' she said, 'but here it is. On the day Aphrodite was born, the gods held a feast. Among the guests was Poros — Resource — the son of Metis, or Cunning. When the feast was over, Penia — Poverty — came to the door to beg, as always happens on such occasions.

Poros, drunk on nectar (there was no wine in those days), wandered into Zeus's garden and fell asleep. Poverty, considering her own desperate situation, decided to conceive a child by him. She lay down beside him and conceived Love. Because Love was conceived on Aphrodite's birthday and is by nature a lover of beauty — and Aphrodite is beautiful — he became her follower and companion. His parentage determines his character. He is always poor — far from tender and beautiful, as most people imagine. He is rough, dirty, barefoot, homeless, sleeping on the ground under the open sky, in doorways and on roadsides. Like his mother, he is always in need. But like his father, he is bold, enterprising, and strong — a tireless hunter, forever scheming, passionate for wisdom, endlessly resourceful. He is a philosopher all his days, a fearsome enchanter, a sorcerer and sophist. By nature he is neither mortal nor immortal: at one moment, when things go well, he is bursting with life; at the next, he is dying — but then he springs back to life again through his father's nature.

What flows into him is always flowing out, so he's never truly rich or truly poor. He stands between wisdom and ignorance. Here is the truth: no god seeks wisdom, because gods are already wise. Nor does anyone who is already wise seek wisdom. But the ignorant don't seek it either — and that's the real evil of ignorance: people who are neither good nor wise are perfectly satisfied with themselves. They don't desire what they don't realize they lack.' 'Then who are the lovers of wisdom, Diotima, if they're neither the wise nor the foolish?' 'Even a child could answer that,' she replied. 'They're the ones in between — and Love is one of them. Wisdom is among the most beautiful things, and Love loves beauty. Therefore Love is a lover of wisdom — a philosopher — standing between the wise and the ignorant. His parentage explains this: his father is wealthy and wise, his mother poor and foolish. That, dear Socrates, is the nature of Love. Your mistake was natural: I think you confused Love with the beloved. The beloved is truly beautiful, delicate, perfect, and blessed. But Love — the principle of love itself — is of a very different nature, as I've described.'

'Well said, wise stranger,' I replied. 'But assuming Love is as you describe, what use is he to humans?' 'That, Socrates, I'll try to explain. I've described his nature and parentage; now, as you acknowledged, Love is the love of beautiful things. But someone might ask: what does the lover of beautiful things desire? What does he want?' 'That the beautiful things become his,' I answered. 'But that answer raises another question: what does possessing beauty give you?' 'I don't have an answer for that,' I admitted. 'Then let me substitute "good" for "beautiful" and ask again: if someone loves the good, what do they want?' 'To possess the good,' I said. 'And what does possessing the good give them?' 'That's easier — happiness,' I replied. 'Yes,' she said, 'the happy are happy because they possess good things. And there's no need to ask further why someone wants happiness — that answer is final.' 'You're right,' I said.

'Is this desire universal? Do all people always desire the good, or only some?' 'All people,' I replied. 'Then why,' she asked, 'don't we say that everyone is in love — if everyone is always loving the same things?' 'I've wondered about that myself,' I said. 'It's not hard to explain,' she replied. 'We take one particular form of love and give it the name that belongs to the whole, while the other forms go by different names.' 'Give me an example,' I said. She answered: 'Consider creation. In its broadest sense, all bringing of something from non-being into being is creation or "making," and everyone who does this is a "maker." Yet we don't call them all makers — only the specific kind who work with music and verse are called "poets," even though all creation is a form of poetry.' 'True,' I said. 'The same applies to love.

In the broadest sense, all desire for the good and for happiness is the great and subtle power of love. But people who pursue the good through money-making, athletics, or philosophy aren't called lovers. The name "lover" is reserved for those whose passion takes one particular form — they alone are said to love.' 'You're probably right,' I said. 'Yes,' she added, 'and you hear people say that lovers are searching for their other half. But I say they're searching neither for a half nor a whole unless that half or whole happens to be good. People will even cut off their own hands and feet if those parts are diseased — what they love isn't what belongs to them, but what is good. Because the only thing people truly love is the good. Do you agree?' 'Absolutely,' I said. 'Then the simple truth is that people love the good.' 'Yes.' 'And they love not just possessing the good but possessing it forever?' 'That too.' 'Then love,' she said, 'can be defined as the desire for the eternal possession of the good.' 'Exactly right.'

'If that's the nature of love,' she continued, 'what form does the pursuit take? What are lovers actually doing — what is the goal behind all this eagerness and passion we call love?' 'If I knew that, Diotima, I wouldn't have needed to come to you as a student.' 'Then I'll tell you. The object of love is birth in beauty — whether of body or soul.' 'That's an oracle that needs explaining,' I said. 'Let me be clearer,' she replied. 'All human beings are pregnant — in body and in soul. When we reach a certain maturity, our nature longs to give birth. But birth can only happen in the presence of beauty, not ugliness. The union of man and woman is a divine act; conception and birth are the immortal element in a mortal creature. These things cannot occur in the presence of discord — and ugliness is always at odds with the divine, while beauty is in harmony with it.

Beauty is the goddess who presides over birth. In the presence of beauty, the creative power is at ease — it opens up, gives birth, and bears fruit. In the presence of ugliness, it contracts, shrinks, turns away in pain, and holds back from conceiving. That's why, when the time for creation is ripe and the creative nature is full, there's such excitement and passion around beauty — beauty's approach relieves the pain of labor. So love, Socrates, is not the love of beauty exactly.' 'What is it then?' 'The love of birth and creation in the presence of beauty.' 'Yes,' I said. 'Absolutely,' she confirmed. 'But why birth and creation?' 'Because for mortal creatures, creation is a kind of eternity and immortality. And since we've agreed that love is the desire for the eternal possession of the good, it follows that love must also be the love of immortality.'

She taught me all this at various times in our conversations about love. Once she said to me: 'What do you think causes love and the desire that goes with it, Socrates? Haven't you noticed how all animals — birds and beasts alike — are seized with a kind of agony when the urge to reproduce takes hold? First comes the desire to mate, then the devotion to offspring — the weakest creatures will fight the strongest to the death and starve themselves to protect their young. You might explain human behavior by reason, but why do animals feel these things so intensely? Can you tell me why?' When I admitted I couldn't, she said: 'Do you expect to master the art of love without understanding this?' 'That's exactly why I came to you, Diotima — I know I need a teacher. Tell me the cause.' 'Don't be surprised,' she said. 'The same principle applies: mortal nature seeks, as far as it can, to be everlasting and immortal. And the only way to achieve this is through reproduction — by always leaving behind a new being in place of the old one.

Even within a single person's life, there's no real permanence — only succession. A person is called the same from youth to old age, but in the short span of a lifetime, every part is always changing: hair, flesh, bones, blood, the entire body. And not just the body — the soul changes too. Habits, character, opinions, desires, pleasures, pains, fears — none of them stay the same in any person. They're constantly appearing and disappearing. Even more remarkable: the same is true of knowledge. Not just that fields of knowledge arise and pass away — so that we're never the same in what we know — but each individual piece of knowledge undergoes the same process. What we call 'remembering' is really the replacement of departed knowledge: forgetting is knowledge leaving, and recollection creates a new copy that seems identical to the old one. This is how all mortal things are preserved — not by remaining absolutely the same, but by substitution. The old gives way to a new version of itself, similar but not identical. This is how mortal beings — the body, and everything mortal — share in immortality. The immortal achieves it differently.
So don't be surprised that every living thing naturally cherishes its offspring. That universal love and care exists for the sake of immortality.'

I was amazed by her words, and said: 'Is this really true, wise Diotima?' She answered with the authority of an expert: 'You can be sure of it, Socrates. Just look at human ambition, and you'll be shocked by its irrationality — unless you understand that people are driven by the love of immortal fame. They're ready to take risks, spend money, endure hardship, and even die for the sake of leaving behind a name that will last forever — risks far greater than they would take for their children. Do you think Alcestis would have died for Admetus, or Achilles for Patroclus, or your own Codrus to save his sons' kingdom, if they hadn't believed that the memory of their virtue would be immortal — which it is, down to our own day? Certainly not,' she said. 'I'm convinced that everyone does everything — and the better they are, the more they do — for the sake of immortal glory. What they desire is the immortal.'

'Those who are pregnant in the body turn to women and beget children — that's the form their love takes. They hope their offspring will preserve their memory and give them the immortal happiness they desire. But there are those who are pregnant in the soul — who conceive things that belong properly to the soul. And what are these conceptions? Wisdom and virtue. All creative people are such soul-parents — especially poets and inventors worthy of the name. But the greatest and most beautiful form of wisdom is the one concerned with ordering cities and households — what we call temperance and justice. When someone carries the seeds of these virtues from youth and is themselves inspired, when maturity comes they long to create and give birth.

Such a person wanders in search of beauty, so they can give birth — because you can't create in the presence of ugliness. When they find a beautiful, noble, and well-formed soul, they embrace that person with all their being. In that person's company they're full of ideas about virtue, about what a good person should be and do. Through contact and conversation with the beautiful, they bring forth what they had been carrying within them, and together they nurture their creation. The bond between such people is far closer than the bond between parents and ordinary children — because the children they share are more beautiful and more enduring. Who would not prefer Homer's and Hesiod's children to human ones? Who wouldn't envy them for leaving behind offspring that have earned them eternal fame? Or consider Lycurgus, who left behind laws that were the salvation not just of Sparta but of all Greece.

Solon, too, is honored as the father of Athenian law. Many others across the Greek and non-Greek world have produced noble works and been parents of every kind of virtue. Temples have been built in their honor — something never done for anyone's mortal children.

'These are the lesser mysteries of love, Socrates, and you could probably master them. But the greater mysteries — the ultimate destination to which these lead, if pursued rightly — I'm not sure you can reach. Still, I'll do my best to explain; try to follow. The person who approaches this correctly should begin in youth by being drawn to beautiful forms. If properly guided, they should first love one particular beautiful body and in that relationship create beautiful ideas. Then they should realize that the beauty in any one body is related to the beauty in all other bodies. Once they see this, they'll relax their intense passion for just one, recognizing it as a small thing, and become a lover of all beautiful forms. Next, they'll come to see that beauty of the soul is more valuable than beauty of the body.

So that if someone with a virtuous soul has even modest physical beauty, the lover will be satisfied — will love and care for them, and will seek to bring forth ideas that improve the young. This will lead them to contemplate the beauty of practices and laws, and to see that all beauty is of one family, and that physical beauty is a small thing. After practices and laws, they'll turn to the sciences and behold their beauty — no longer enslaved to the beauty of one person, one practice, one field of knowledge like a petty servant, but gazing out at the vast ocean of beauty. In that contemplation they'll produce many beautiful and noble thoughts in the boundless love of wisdom, until at last they grow strong enough to perceive a single science — the science of beauty itself. Now pay very close attention:

'The person who has been guided this far in love — who has learned to see beautiful things in their proper order and progression — will suddenly, near the end of the journey, catch sight of something wonderfully beautiful in its nature. This, Socrates, is what all our earlier efforts have been building toward. This beauty is, first of all, eternal — it doesn't come into being or perish, doesn't grow or diminish. Second, it's not beautiful from one angle and ugly from another, not beautiful at one time and not at another, not beautiful in relation to one thing and ugly in relation to something else, not beautiful here but ugly there, not beautiful to some people and ugly to others. It won't appear as a face, or hands, or any bodily part, or as any speech or piece of knowledge, or as existing in any particular thing — not in an animal, not in the earth, not in the sky, not anywhere. It exists purely in itself, by itself, uniform and eternal. Every other beautiful thing participates in this beauty, but in such a way that while other things come into being and perish, this beauty neither increases nor decreases nor undergoes any change. Whoever ascends from particular beauties through the power of true love begins to glimpse this beauty — that person is approaching the end.

The correct path — whether you walk it yourself or are led by another — is to start from the beauties of this world and ascend always upward toward that ultimate beauty. You use earthly beauties as stepping stones: from one beautiful body to two, from two to all beautiful bodies, from beautiful bodies to beautiful practices, from practices to beautiful ideas, and from ideas to the idea of beauty itself — until at last you know what beauty truly is. This, dear Socrates,' said the woman from Mantineia, 'is the life worth living above all others — the life spent contemplating absolute beauty. Once you saw it, you would never again compare it to gold, fine clothes, or beautiful young people — whose presence now entrances you so much that you and many others would gladly go without food and drink just to gaze at them and be near them. But what if you could see true beauty — divine beauty, pure and clear, uncorrupted by human flesh and color and all the other mortal nonsense — what if you could behold beauty itself, simple and divine?

Remember: only in contemplating that beauty with the mind's eye will a person be able to give birth not to images of virtue but to true virtue itself — because they are grasping not an image but the real thing. And by bringing forth and nurturing true virtue, they will become beloved of God and, as much as any mortal can, become immortal themselves. Would that be an unworthy life?'

Such, Phaedrus — and I speak not only to you but to all of you — were the words of Diotima. I was persuaded of their truth. And being persuaded, I try to persuade others that in pursuing this goal, human nature will not easily find a better helper than Love. Therefore every person should honor Love as I do, and follow his ways, and encourage others to do the same, praising his power and spirit as best they can — now and always.
The words I have spoken, Phaedrus, you may call a eulogy of Love — or whatever you like.

When Socrates finished, everyone applauded. Aristophanes was about to respond to something Socrates had said about his earlier speech when suddenly there was a tremendous banging at the front door — the sound of revelers — and the notes of a flute-girl. Agathon told the servants to go see who it was. 'If they're friends, invite them in. If not, tell them the drinking is over.' Soon they heard the voice of Alcibiades booming through the courtyard — extremely drunk, shouting: 'Where's Agathon? Take me to Agathon!' Finally, supported by the flute-girl and some attendants, he appeared at the door, crowned with a thick garland of ivy and violets, ribbons streaming from his head. 'Greetings, friends!' he called. 'Will you welcome a very drunk man to your party? Or shall I just crown Agathon — which is why I came — and go? I couldn't make it yesterday, so here I am today with these ribbons on my head, planning to transfer them to the head of the fairest and wisest man — if I may call him that. Will you laugh at me for being drunk? Go ahead — I know I'm speaking the truth. But first, tell me: on these terms, may I come in?
Will you drink with me or not?'

Everyone clamored for him to come in and take a seat. Agathon invited him warmly. His companions led him in, and as he walked, intending to crown Agathon, he held the ribbons in front of his eyes — which prevented him from seeing Socrates. He took the empty space between Agathon and Socrates, Socrates having moved aside to make room. Sitting down, he embraced Agathon and crowned him. 'Take off his sandals,' said Agathon, 'so he can be a third on our couch.'

'Gladly! But who's this third person?' said Alcibiades, turning around — and then starting back as he caught sight of Socrates. 'By Heracles! What's this? Socrates! You're lying in ambush again, popping up where I least expect you — as always. What are you doing here? And how did you manage to get a seat not next to Aristophanes or some other comedian, but next to the best-looking person in the room?'

Socrates turned to Agathon: 'Protect me, Agathon! This man's passion for me has become a serious problem. Ever since I became his admirer, I haven't been allowed to look at or talk to anyone attractive without him flying into a jealous rage. He abuses me, and I'm half afraid he'll actually attack me. Please, either reconcile us or defend me if he gets violent — I'm genuinely frightened of his obsessive love.'

'There can be no reconciliation between you and me,' said Alcibiades. 'I'll punish you for that later. But for now, Agathon, give me some of those ribbons back — I need to crown this extraordinary head as well. He mustn't complain that I crowned you and neglected him — the man who conquers everyone in conversation, and not just once like you the other day, but all the time.' Taking some ribbons, he crowned Socrates and reclined again.

'You all seem far too sober,' he declared, 'and that won't do. You must drink — those were the terms of my admission. I appoint myself master of the feast until you're all properly drunk. Agathon, let's have a large goblet — or better yet,' he said, spotting a wine-cooler that held more than two quarts, 'bring me that.' He filled it, drained it, and ordered it refilled for Socrates. 'Watch this, friends,' said Alcibiades. 'My trick won't work on Socrates — he can drink any amount and never get drunk.' Socrates drank what was poured for him.
'What's this, Alcibiades?' said Eryximachus. 'Are we just going to gulp wine in silence, with no conversation or singing? Are we drinking like people dying of thirst?'
'Hail, worthy son of a most wise and worthy father!' replied Alcibiades.
'The same to you,' said Eryximachus. 'But what shall we do?'
'Whatever you prescribe,' said Alcibiades.
'The wise physician, skilled our wounds to heal —'
shall give us our orders, and we'll obey. What do you want?'

'Well,' said Eryximachus, 'before you arrived, we'd agreed that each of us would make a speech praising Love, going from left to right. Everyone has spoken except you — though you've certainly drunk your share. It's only fair that you give a speech, and then assign Socrates whatever topic you like, and he'll assign one to his neighbor on the right, and so on.'

'That sounds fine, Eryximachus,' said Alcibiades, 'but it's hardly fair to match a drunk man against sober speakers. Also, my dear friend, did you actually believe anything Socrates just said? The truth is the exact opposite: if I praise anyone but him in his presence — god or mortal — he can barely keep his hands off me.'
'Shame on you,' said Socrates.
'Hold your tongue,' said Alcibiades. 'By Poseidon, I will praise no one but you while you're in the room.'
'Then do it,' said Eryximachus. 'Praise Socrates, if you like.'
'You mean it?' said Alcibiades. 'Shall I attack him and exact my revenge in front of everyone?'
'What are you planning?' said Socrates. 'Going to mock me? Is that what your praise amounts to?'
'I'm going to speak the truth, if you'll let me.'
'I not only let you — I urge you to speak the truth.'

'Here goes, then,' said Alcibiades. 'And if I say anything untrue, stop me and say "That's a lie" — though I intend only to tell the truth. But don't be surprised if I jump around from topic to topic. It's not easy for a drunk man to give a smooth, orderly account of all your peculiarities.'

Now, friends, I'm going to praise Socrates through a comparison that will seem like a caricature — but I'm speaking for truth's sake, not to mock him. I say he is exactly like those statues of Silenus you see in sculptors' shops — the ones holding pipes and flutes that open up in the middle to reveal images of gods inside. I also say he resembles the satyr Marsyas. You won't deny, Socrates, that your face is like a satyr's. And the resemblance goes deeper. You're a bully — I can prove it with witnesses if you deny it. And aren't you a flute-player? A far more astonishing one than Marsyas. He used the power of instruments to charm people's souls, and those who play his melodies still do — whether performed by a virtuoso or a mediocre flute-girl, the tunes of Olympus (which came from Marsyas) have a power no others possess. They alone seize the soul and reveal who needs the gods and their mysteries, because those melodies are divine. But you produce the same effect with nothing but words — no instruments needed. That's the difference between you and Marsyas.

When we hear any other speaker, even a brilliant one, nobody is much affected. But the mere fragments of your words — even secondhand, even badly repeated — amaze and possess the soul of everyone who hears them, man, woman, or child. If I weren't afraid you'd think me hopelessly drunk, I'd swear to the effect your words have always had on me. When I hear you, my heart pounds harder than any Corybantic worshipper's, and tears pour from my eyes. I've seen others react the same way. I've heard Pericles and other great orators — they spoke well, but they never made me feel like this. They never made my soul revolt against itself, never made me feel ashamed of the way I live. But this satyr has often brought me to the point where life seemed unbearable.
