And I know that if I don't block my ears and run from him like from a Siren, I'll spend the rest of my life sitting at his feet. He makes me admit that I neglect my own soul while busying myself with Athenian politics. So I force myself to tear away from him.

He is the only person who has ever made me feel ashamed — which you might not think is in my nature. No one else can do it. I know I can't answer him or deny that I should do what he says. But the moment I leave his presence, the love of popularity wins me over again. So I run from him and avoid him. When I see him, I'm ashamed of what I once confessed to him. Many times I've wished he were dead — and yet I know I'd be far more miserable if he died. I don't know what to do with the man.

That's what this satyr's flute-playing has done to me and to many others. But hear one more thing — let me show you how exact the comparison is and how extraordinary his power. None of you truly know him. But I will reveal him, since I've begun. You see how he's always chasing beautiful people, always smitten with them — and at the same time how he claims to know nothing, to be completely ignorant. Isn't that Silenus-like? Absolutely — it's his outer shell, like the carved Silenus head. But if you open him up, my fellow drinkers, and look inside — what self-control you'll find in there! Beauty, wealth, and honor — the things most people admire — mean nothing to him. He utterly despises them. He considers all of us worthless. His whole life is one long performance of ironic pretense before the world. But when I opened him up and looked at his inner seriousness, I found images inside so divine and golden and beautiful that I was ready to do whatever Socrates asked of me. Others may not have noticed them, but I did. I once thought he was genuinely attracted to my beauty, and I considered this a wonderful opportunity to hear everything he knew. I had quite a high opinion of my own attractiveness.

With this plan in mind, I went to see him and sent away my usual attendant — I'll tell the whole truth; listen carefully, and Socrates, if I lie, call me out. So there we were, alone together. I thought he'd finally speak to me the way lovers speak when they're alone with their beloved, and I was thrilled. Nothing of the sort. He talked to me just as he always did, spent the day with me, and left. I then challenged him to exercise together at the gymnasium. He wrestled with me several times when no one else was around — but I got nowhere. Finally, having failed at everything, I decided I had to be direct and bold. I'd started this pursuit and I wouldn't give up until I knew where I stood. I invited him to dinner — like a lover setting a trap for a beautiful youth. He was hard to persuade, but eventually he came. The first time, he wanted to leave right after dinner, and I was too embarrassed to stop him. But I tried again. After the second dinner, I kept the conversation going deep into the night. When he wanted to leave, I insisted it was too late and he should stay.

He lay down on the couch next to me — the same one he'd eaten on — and we were the only ones in the room. Everything I've said so far could be told without shame. But what comes next, I wouldn't tell if I were sober. Yet as they say, 'in wine there is truth' — and I must speak. Besides, it would be wrong to hide Socrates' extraordinary conduct when I'm supposed to be praising him. And I speak as someone bitten by a snake — and as they say, only those who have been bitten understand the pain and will forgive what it drives you to say and do. I have been bitten by something worse than a viper — bitten in my soul, my heart, or whatever you want to call it — bitten by philosophy, which stings harder than any serpent, especially in a young and impressionable soul. It makes you say and do wild things. And all of you here — Phaedrus, Agathon, Eryximachus, Pausanias, Aristodemus, Aristophanes, and Socrates himself — you've all felt the same madness, the same philosophical frenzy. So you'll understand and forgive me. But the servants and anyone else who is crude or uninitiated — plug your ears.

When the lamp was out and the servants had gone, I decided to stop being coy and speak plainly. I gave him a shake and said: 'Socrates, are you asleep?' 'No,' he said. 'Do you know what I've been thinking?' 'What?' 'I've decided that of all the lovers I've ever had, you alone are worthy of me — and you seem too modest to say anything about it. So let me be frank: I'd be a fool to refuse you this or any other favor. I'm offering you everything I have and everything my friends have, in hopes that you'll help me become the best person I can be. I believe you can help me more than anyone else. And I'd be far more ashamed to be judged foolish by wise men for refusing someone like you than to be judged by the foolish majority for accepting.' He replied with that characteristic irony of his: 'My dear Alcibiades, you really do have lofty ambitions — if what you say about me is true, if I really do have some power to make you better. You must see in me a beauty infinitely superior to your own good looks. And if you're trying to trade your beauty for mine — appearance for reality — you're getting much the better deal. It's gold for bronze, as Homer would say.

But look more carefully, my friend, and make sure you're not mistaken about me. The mind's eye grows sharper when the physical eye begins to fade — and you have a long way to go before that happens.' Hearing this, I said: 'I've told you what I think, and I mean it. Now it's your turn to decide what's best for both of us.' 'Good,' he said. 'We'll think about it another time and act as seems best.' Having heard this, I thought my words had struck home like arrows. Without waiting to hear more, I got up, threw my coat over him, crept under his threadbare cloak — it was winter — and lay there all night with my arms around this extraordinary being. Again, Socrates will not deny this. And yet, despite everything, he was so utterly unmoved by my advances, so contemptuous and dismissive of my beauty — which I actually thought was worth something — that, I swear by all the gods, when I got up in the morning, nothing had happened. I might as well have been sleeping next to my father or an older brother.

Can you imagine how I felt after that rejection? Dishonored — and yet in awe of his character, his self-control, his extraordinary strength of mind. I never imagined I'd encounter a man like this — so wise and so disciplined. I couldn't be angry at him or give up his company, any more than I could hope to win him over. I knew that money couldn't touch him — just as weapons couldn't touch Ajax — and my one strategy for winning him, my physical beauty, had failed completely. I was utterly enslaved and helpless. All this happened before we both went on the military expedition to Potidaea, where we shared a mess. There I could observe his incredible endurance. When supply lines were cut and we had to go hungry — something that happens often in war — he surpassed not just me but everyone. And at feasts, he was the only one who truly enjoyed himself. He didn't want to drink, but when pushed, he outdrank us all — and here's the astonishing thing: no one has ever seen Socrates drunk. You may get a chance to test that soon. His resistance to cold was equally remarkable.

There was a terrible frost — the winters in that region are brutal — and everyone either stayed indoors or went out wrapped in extraordinary quantities of clothing with their feet swaddled in felt and sheepskin. Socrates marched through it all barefoot, in his ordinary clothes, more easily than the soldiers with shoes. They glared at him, thinking he was mocking them.
I've told you one story; now let me tell you another, worth hearing —
'Of the deeds and endurance of this remarkable man'

while on the campaign. One morning he began puzzling over something and couldn't solve it. He wouldn't give up, but stood there thinking from dawn until noon. People noticed, and word spread through the amazed crowd: 'Socrates has been standing in one spot thinking since sunrise.' Finally, in the evening after dinner, some Ionians — curious to see if he'd stand all night — brought their bedrolls outside and watched him. (This was summer, not winter.) He stood there until the next morning. At dawn, he said a prayer to the sun and walked away. I should also tell you about his courage in battle — who else but Socrates saved my life? I was wounded in the battle where I received my medal for valor, and he refused to leave me. He rescued both me and my armor. He should have received the medal — the generals wanted to give it to me partly because of my rank — and I told them as much. Socrates won't deny this. But he was more eager for me to receive the honor than to receive it himself.

On another occasion — the retreat after the battle of Delium — I saw him behave magnificently. I was on horseback, so relatively safe, while he was retreating on foot with Laches, the troops in full flight. I met them and told them not to lose heart, promising to stay with them. And there you could see him — just as Aristophanes describes him in the streets of Athens — striding along like a pelican, eyes rolling calmly, surveying friends and enemies alike. It was obvious to everyone, even at a distance, that anyone who attacked this man would meet fierce resistance. That's how he and his companion escaped safely. In war, people who keep their composure are rarely attacked; it's those who run in panic who get cut down. I saw many remarkable things about Socrates that day.

You might compare Brasidas or others to Achilles, or Nestor and Antenor to Pericles — and find reasonable parallels for other famous men. But for this strange being you will never find a likeness — not among people alive today or anyone who has ever lived — unless you compare him, as I have, to the Sileni and satyrs. And the comparison extends not just to him but to his words. I forgot to mention this earlier: his words, too, are like those Silenus statues that open up. When you first hear them, they seem ridiculous — he talks about pack-donkeys, blacksmiths, cobblers, and tanners, always saying the same things in the same words. Any naive listener would laugh. But open those words up and look inside, and you'll find they are the only words that truly make sense — the most divine words, containing the most images of virtue, covering the broadest range of human concerns — in fact, everything a person who wants to become good and noble needs to think about.

That, friends, is my praise of Socrates — mixed in with my complaint about how he's mistreated me. And I'm not the only one. He's done the same to Charmides, Euthydemus, and many others — starting out as their lover and ending up making them pursue him instead. Be warned, Agathon: learn from my experience. Don't be fooled by him. Don't be, as the proverb says, a fool who has to learn the hard way.

When Alcibiades finished, everyone laughed at his frankness — he obviously was still in love with Socrates. 'You're more sober than you let on, Alcibiades,' said Socrates. 'Otherwise you wouldn't have been so clever about wrapping your real purpose inside all that elaborate praise. You slipped it in at the very end, as an afterthought — as though the whole speech wasn't really designed to make Agathon and me quarrel. You want me to love only you, and Agathon to be loved only by you. But your little satyr play has been seen through. Agathon, don't let him drive a wedge between us.'
'I think you're right,' said Agathon. 'His sitting between us was clearly meant to separate us. But it won't work — I'll come and lie on the couch next to you.'
'Yes, yes,' said Socrates, 'come here and lie below me.'
'Again!' cried Alcibiades. 'How this man defeats me at every turn! At least, I beg you, let Agathon lie between us.'

'Impossible,' said Socrates. 'You praised me, and now I must praise the person on my right — that's the order we established. If Agathon lies between us, he'd have to praise me again instead of being praised by me. And I very much want to praise this young man. Let it be.'
'Wonderful!' cried Agathon. 'I'll move at once — I can't wait to be praised by Socrates.'
'The usual story,' sighed Alcibiades. 'Wherever Socrates is, no one else has a chance with the beautiful. And look how easily he's found a plausible reason to draw Agathon to his side.'

chapters.title: Alcibiades
paragraphs: Agathon was getting up to take a place on the couch beside Socrates when suddenly a crowd of revelers burst in, throwing the whole party into confusion. Someone leaving had left the front door open, and they poured in without ceremony. The noise was tremendous, all order vanished, and everyone was forced to drink enormous quantities of wine. Aristodemus said that Eryximachus, Phaedrus, and some others left at that point, while he himself fell asleep and slept for a long time — the nights were long at that season. He woke near dawn, as the cocks were crowing, and saw that most of the company were either asleep or had gone. Only Agathon, Aristophanes, and Socrates were still awake, drinking from a large bowl that they passed around from left to right. Socrates was arguing with them. Aristodemus couldn't remember most of what was said — he'd missed the beginning and was still half asleep — but the gist was that Socrates was forcing them to admit that the same person could be skilled at writing both comedy and tragedy, and that a true master of tragedy must also be a master of comedy. They were being compelled to agree, though they weren't entirely following the argument and kept nodding off. Aristophanes fell asleep first, and then, as daylight was breaking, Agathon. Socrates, having put them both to sleep, got up and left. Aristodemus followed him, as was his habit. Socrates went to the Lyceum, bathed, and spent the rest of the day as usual. In the evening, he went home to bed.
